title: Chorus grows  for IMF continuity | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 05:18
-     - 15

Standard Chartered Bank Sri Lanka CEO Bingumal Thewarathanthri

Advocata Institute Chairman Murtaza Jafferjee

By Charumini de Silva

The chorus for continuity of an International Monetary Fund (IMF) program is growing judging by sentiments expressed by two business and thought leaders at the Daily FT-Colombo University MBA Alumni Association post-Budget forum on Friday.

Advocata Institute Chairman Murtaza Jafferjee, a panellist at the forum, called for Sri Lanka to pursue an 18th IMF program, after the current $ 2.9 billion four-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) concludes in March 2027.

He said that an arrangement would provide a crucial financial safety net against an increasingly volatile global environment, even as the economy recovers.

In responding to a question at the post-Budget Forum, Jafferjee recalled that he had once toasted at a forum with the Treasury Secretary in attendance, that the 17th IMF program should be Sri Lanka’s last.

“I completely reverse my toast, not because we are in trouble, but because the world around us has turned nasty,” Jafferjee said, at the Forum, where Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma was also in the panel following his keynote.

Jafferjee pointed out that the rising global borrowing costs, with US 10-year Treasury yields reaching 5%, would shape the rates at which Sri Lanka can borrow. 

“Borrowing from the IMF is much cheaper,” he said, adding that an arrangement with the Fund would act as a confidence signal to international credit markets. 

Jafferjee also said it will provide priority access to technical assistance, which remains fundamental to Sri Lanka’s institutional and economic development. 

Another panellist, Standard Chartered Bank Sri Lanka CEO Bingumal Thewarathanthri, was also supportive of a new IMF program given external uncertainties in the future, but was vary over some espousing the need for IMF for monitoring the country.

Thewarathanthri said a future program with the IMF depends on Sri Lanka’s comfort in managing a ‘black swan’ event. 

“If there is a prolonged crisis in West Asia, we might have to be in a program. In normal conditions, the country could discuss something like a short-term Stand-By-Agreement (SBA), but it must shed the idea that we need the IMF to monitor us,” which he called a ‘bad psychology to have.’

He credited citizens and policymakers delivering ‘beyond expected results’, but cautioned that any new program must reflect domestic economic and social realities, as a large share of the population remains vulnerable despite improvements in macroeconomic indicators. 

Thewarathanthri also said past IMF-related pushback, such as on property tax, shows that conditions have to fit the country.

Treasury Secretary Dr. Suriyapperuma said, the Government signalled its approach in the Budget speech and has appointed a high-level committee to examine the options and the engagement modalities available to make recommendations. 

“The approach will rest on information and data, including the level of reserves built so far and projected reserves accumulation and all of this will be factored in when the committee’s report is finalised,” he added. 

When asked about criticism that strong macro numbers are not being felt by households, with poverty and purchasing power complaints rising, Dr. Suriyapperuma said the Government had to intervene twice this year because inflation is closely tied to the energy prices and Sri Lanka is dependent on imports.

title: Lakdhanavi secures  $ 75 m contract to build 57 MW power plant in India | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 05:16
-     - 7

Lakdhanavi Ltd., a member of the LTL Group, has signed a turnkey Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contract worth approximately Rs. 25 billion ($ 75 million) to build a 57 MW natural gas-based fired power plant on India’s Andaman Island.

LTL Group is the largest power sector company in Sri Lanka with interests in power generation, transmission, and also distribution. Originally set up as a joint venture between the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) and a European company, currently National Transmission Network System Provider Ltd., (NTNSP), a Government-owned entity under the Energy Ministry, holds 35% stake in LTL Holdings Ltd.

The contract was awarded by NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Ltd., (NVVN), a wholly owned subsidiary of National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) Ltd., which is owned by the Government of India, following an international competitive bidding (ICB) process in which Lakdhanavi emerged as the lowest priced bidder (L1).

The contract was signed in September at the NTPC Office Complex in Noida, New Delhi, in the presence of senior representatives of NVVN, Lakdhanavi, and LTL Holdings. The parties also discussed project implementation and future collaboration between NVVN and Lakdhanavi.

A milestone for Sri Lankan engineering

The project will be located at Hope Town, Port Blair, in Andaman Island and is expected to strengthen the island’s electricity infrastructure, enable long-term energy security through LNG infrastructure, and facilitate future economic development. The Lakdhanavi Ltd., engineering team would be responsible for the execution of the project, with Wärtsilä Corporation of Finland being the supplier of the power-generating equipment to Lakdhanavi Ltd.

The award marks Lakdhanavi’s entry into India’s power plant EPC market and further expands its regional presence. Established in Sri Lanka in the late 90s as a subsidiary of LTL Holdings, the company has decades of experience in power generation as an Independent Power Producer (IPP) and a provider of Operations and Maintenance (O&M) solutions for thermal and renewable energy projects. Its overseas power project experience includes projects in Bangladesh, Nepal, and the Maldives.

Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka met LTL’s management and expressed the Government’s delight over this achievement, welcoming the success of a Sri Lankan company in securing a major infrastructure contract in a large and competitive market such as India. This underscored the national significance of the achievement and the value of Sri Lankan companies taking their expertise to international markets.

Beyond its commercial significance, the project is a practical reflection of longstanding economic ties between Sri Lanka and India. While bilateral economic engagement has often been viewed through the lens of Indian investment, development assistance, and infrastructure participation in Sri Lanka, Lakdhanavi’s success demonstrates that opportunities can arise in both directions and that Sri Lankan companies should pursue them with diligence.

The contract demonstrates how Sri Lankan businesses can contribute their skills and capabilities for mutual development of both countries, complementing the close cooperation of the two Governments with tangible private-sector partnerships. It offers an encouraging example of how the two neighbouring countries can deepen economic cooperation and create mutually benefitting opportunities.

Lakdhanavi Ltd., and LTL Holdings CEO Eng. Nuhuman Marikkar described the contract as a significant milestone for the company and a notable achievement for Sri Lankan engineering. He said the award reflected the strength of the company’s technical capabilities, the dedication of its team, and the confidence placed in its ability to deliver complex power infrastructure projects successfully, both in its home market and elsewhere.

He added that Lakdhanavi is looking forward to working closely with NVVN to deliver the project successfully.

title: Institutional analysts say Budget 2027 broadly toes fiscal line, warn of post-IMF tests | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 05:13
-     - 12

Budget 2027, presented by President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake on 12 November, keeps the country on its fiscal consolidation path, with a primary surplus that just meets the International Monetary Fund (IMF) target. 

However, leading investment houses warn that a wider deficit, a 35% jump in capital spending, and the end of the IMF program in March 2027 will test the Government’s fiscal discipline, pointing to the Government’s good sense to explore alternatives with the IMF post-Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program.

Reviews by HNB Stockbrokers, CT Smith, Softlogic Stockbrokers, First Capital Research, and accounting and tax firm Evolve broadly agree that the Budget avoids major tax changes and stays close to the IMF framework.

 Revenue and grants are budgeted at Rs. 6.18 trillion, up 3.3%. Expenditure is budgeted at Rs. 7.93 trillion, up 8.5%, including a Rs. 260 billion supplementary estimate for Cyclone Ditwah reconstruction. The overall deficit widens to 4.5% of GDP from 3.7% in 2026. The primary surplus, which is revenue minus all spending except interest, narrows to 2.3% of GDP from 3.6%.

First Capital Research said fiscal discipline remains intact, with the deficit comfortably within the Government’s target of below 5% of GDP. “The 2027 Budget maintains Sri Lanka’s medium-term fiscal consolidation path while allowing a temporary increase in public investment to support growth, disaster recovery, and economic modernisation,” it said.

First Capital’s comparison with IMF projections shows where the gap lies. The Budget sets total expenditure at 20.3% of GDP, against the IMF’s 18.7%. Capital expenditure is 5.1% of GDP, against the IMF’s 4%. The deficit is 4.5% of GDP, 0.8 percentage points wider than the IMF’s 3.7% for 2027. Revenue, at 15.8% of GDP, is above the IMF’s 15.1%. First Capital also noted that the gross borrowing requirement is higher. 

“Despite increased spending, the gross borrowing requirement is estimated slightly higher at Rs. 3.8 trillion, with the Ditwah supplementary expenditure expected to be financed from existing cash buffers,” it said.

Softlogic Stockbrokers took the most upbeat view. It described the fiscal framework as broadly aligned with IMF objectives and called the Rs. 2 trillion of public investment particularly encouraging. “We view the 2027 Budget as growth-oriented, marking a shift from stabilisation towards investment-led growth,” Softlogic said. “We are also positive about the Government’s commitment to maintaining fiscal discipline and considering a successor IMF program beyond the current EFF, due to conclude in March 2027.” 

Softlogic pointed to Fitch’s upgrade of Sri Lanka’s rating to B- from CCC+, with a Stable Outlook. It said the upgrade strengthens the case that the macro recovery is becoming more durable, but added that effective implementation and private sector participation will be key.

HNB Stockbrokers said the primary surplus just meets the IMF target. It warned that the margin for error narrows once the EFF ends and Sri Lanka is likely to return to international Bond markets. 

“Continued fiscal discipline remains key to sustaining improving fiscal dynamics and building buffers with a view to securing credit rating upgrades as the IMF program comes to an end, particularly in the backdrop of heightened external risks,” it said. HNB Stockbrokers noted that Sri Lanka’s term premium remains elevated against higher-rated peers, which would raise the cost of new borrowing. The term premium is the extra yield investors demand to hold longer-dated debt.

On revenue, HNB Stockbrokers said the decline to 15.8% of GDP from 16.6% leaves it slightly below the Government’s medium-term target of at least 16%. The decline reflects tax relief measures and fading vehicle import revenue. 

HNB Stockbrokers estimates that taxes other than vehicle-related taxes must grow by 7.6% to meet the Rs. 5.69 trillion tax target. It considers this feasible given expected nominal GDP growth of 7% to 8% and continued efforts to widen the tax net through digitisation. CT Smith put the annual cost of tax relief measures at Rs. 28.4 billion. It noted that income tax is only 23.6% of tax revenue, against the Government’s stated aim of a 40:60 direct-to-indirect tax ratio.

Debt service remains the heaviest burden. Interest costs are budgeted at Rs. 2.64 trillion, or 6.8% of GDP, and account for a third of total expenditure. CT Smith said interest will absorb 43% of revenue, down from 79.1% in 2022. HNB Stockbrokers said the ratio has plateaued at around 43% to 46% since 2025 and is still roughly three times the peer average, well above safe levels. First Capital noted that Central Government debt fell from 114% of GDP in 2022 to 95% in 2025, and that the IMF projects 87% by 2032.

The biggest test lies in capital spending, which rises 35% to Rs. 2 trillion, or 5.1% of GDP, from 4.1%. “Key risk is execution, not funding,” CT Smith said. “Capital spending has a record of falling short of plan.” CT Smith said about 75% of the 2025 capital budget was spent and only about 30% of the 2026 allocation was used in the first nine months. 

CT Smith also said primary expenditure of 13.6% of GDP exceeds the 13% statutory ceiling in 2027, with a return to about 12.9% projected from 2028. HNB Stockbrokers pointed out that underspending could help the fiscal numbers. If capital expenditure falls short of budget as in previous years, the primary surplus is likely to be higher, giving a further fiscal buffer.

HNB Stockbrokers also flagged recurrent spending as a medium-term risk. “We note, however, that the planned recruitment of a further c. 110,000 public sector employees has the potential to undermine fiscal discipline in the coming years,” it said.

Financing has implications for interest rates. Evolve said Rs. 1.38 trillion of the Rs. 1.49 trillion deficit before the supplementary estimate will come from the domestic non-bank market. “Nearly all of the gap is borrowed domestically, which is why interest stays the biggest line,” Evolve said. “For a business, that is the Budget’s clearest signal on where interest rates are heading: the State remains the biggest borrower in town.” CT Smith said net domestic financing rises 45.7% to Rs. 1.64 trillion, of which Rs. 260 billion is drawn from the Treasury cash buffer.

HNB Stockbrokers estimates gross financing needs (GFN) at about 14% of GDP in 2027. GFN is the total the Government must borrow to cover the deficit and maturing debt. HNB Stockbrokers expects it to peak at about 15% in 2028 as large Bond maturities fall due, and to average about 13% over 2027-32, around the benchmark set under the IMF program. Yields rose across the curve after the Central Bank’s 100-basis-point policy rate hike to 8.75% in May 2026. HNB Stockbrokers expects Bond rates to decline gradually as credit growth moderates and consolidation continues, assuming no further external shocks.

The post-IMF path remains open. CT Smith said a committee is to report on whether Sri Lanka should enter another IMF program. It listed October 2026 inflation of 8.3% and an El Niño forecast to peak in February 2027 among the risks to watch.

HNB Stockbrokers said the Budget is likely to be viewed as broadly neutral for the stock market, with no major adverse measures. It described the market and economic outlook as broadly positive but contingent on further building internal and external buffers amid heightened geopolitical risks. Evolve cautioned that the tax measures are still subject to enactment. “Everything here is a proposal until the Bills pass,” it said.

title: SEC says Budget 2027 will boost capital market | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 05:13
-     - 11

Chairman Senior Prof. Hareendra Dissabandara

The Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka (SEC) has welcomed the 2027 Budget, saying the adoption of two of its long-advocated proposals, “A Share for Everyone” and the SME Listing Support Mechanism, will deepen the capital market and broaden investor participation.

“These are not merely Budget proposals. They are investments in Sri Lanka’s future investors, future entrepreneurs, and future economic growth."

The SEC is proud that these longstanding proposals have been taken into consideration, and we remain committed to ensuring their successful implementation for the benefit of the nation,” SEC Chairman Senior Prof. Hareendra Dissabandara said.

The SEC said participation in the capital market remains relatively low compared with the country’s full potential, and that the two initiatives address this from both the supply and demand sides.

“While ‘A Share for Everyone’ aims to expand the investor base and build a stronger investment culture, the SME Listing Support Mechanism will encourage more businesses to enter the market, thereby increasing the diversity and depth of investment opportunities available to Sri Lankan investors,” Prof. Dissabandara said.

“A Share for Everyone”, introduced under the vision “Let’s Know, Let’s Learn, Let’s Invest”, targets young Sri Lankans in school.

“By providing eligible Advanced Level students with an opportunity to enter the capital market and gain first-hand exposure to investing, the program will enhance financial literacy, promote long-term wealth creation, and foster a culture of informed investment among young Sri Lankans,” he said.

The SEC said helping Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) raise capital through stock market listings would give them new avenues for growth, improve corporate governance standards and transparency, and create a broader range of investment opportunities for the public. It described SMEs as the backbone of the economy, contributing significantly to employment, innovation and regional development.

The Commission said it put forward the proposals as part of its statutory role of advising the Government on the development of the securities market. It welcomed the allocation of resources for the initiatives and the collaborative approach involving the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) and other market stakeholders.

The SEC said it will work with the Finance Ministry, the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE), market intermediaries, educational institutions and industry stakeholders to implement the programs, adding that a broader investor community and a wider range of listed companies would improve capital mobilisation, financial inclusion, market liquidity and long-term economic resilience.

title: Tourism earnings rise for third consecutive month in October, but 10-month revenue remains down 8.3% | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 05:12
-     - 12

Sri Lanka’s tourism earnings registered a third consecutive monthly increase in October, rising 3.5% year-on-year (YoY) to $ 192.7 million, after recording its highest-ever monthly tourist arrivals during the month, welcoming 168,625 visitors as demand strengthened ahead of the winter season, according to the latest data released by the Central Bank.

However, the latest monthly gain has yet to reverse the broader weakness in the sector. Tourism earnings during the first 10 months of 2026 fell 8.3% YoY to $ 2.43 billion, compared with $ 2.65 billion in the corresponding period last year. 

The earnings figures have been affected by the SLTDA’s revision of its estimates for tourists’ average daily expenditure and length of stay from October 2025, making comparisons with earlier periods more challenging.

Tourism revenue has also faced pressure amid geopolitical uncertainty and the impact of the conflict involving the US-Israel and Iran, which escalated on 28 February 2026. 

Although the consecutive monthly increases offer some indication of improvement, the decline in cumulative earnings highlights the continuing challenge of translating visitor arrivals into stronger tourism receipts.

The Government has appointed Dheera Hettiarachchi, as Acting Chairman of the Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau (SLTPB).

Industry sources confirmed the move, though no formal announcement had been made at the time of reporting. The appointment follows the resignation last month of SLTPB Chairman Buddhika Hewawasam (https://www.ft.lk/front-page/SLTPB-Chairman-Buddhika-Hewawasam-resigns/44-799539). 

Hettiarachchi now heads three key institutions under Sri Lanka Tourism; Sri Lanka Institute of Tourism and Hotel Management (SLITHM), the Sri Lanka Convention Bureau (SLCB), and SLTPB. The Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) is headed by Suranjith Wewita, who was appointed Chairman in August following Hewawasam’s resignation from that post (https://www.ft.lk/front-page/Hewawasam-resigns-as-SLTDA-Chairman/44-796136) 

The leadership change comes as Sri Lanka steps up efforts to regain momentum in international markets, with interim, market-specific promotional campaigns planned ahead of the winter travel season. These initiatives are expected to sustain destination visibility until the proposed Rs. 3.5 billion global destination branding campaign begins in early 2027.

With the SLTPB central to destination marketing and international positioning, the industry is awaiting greater clarity on the leadership and implementation of the country’s broader tourism promotion strategy.

title: People’s Bank sustains strong earnings momentum | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 05:07

Chairman Chandana Guniyangoda (left) and CEO/GM Clive Fonseka

People’s Bank has delivered a strong financial performance for the nine months ended 30 September 2026, building on its earnings momentum and demonstrating financial resilience in an evolving global and domestic economic environment. 

The bank achieved a standalone Profit Before Tax (PBT) of Rs. 52.1 billion, supported by sustained core banking performance, prudent balance sheet management, and disciplined credit and risk management. This performance underscores the strength of the bank’s financial fundamentals and its ability to sustain progress while navigating changing economic and geopolitical conditions.

Strong growth across core income streams reinforced the bank’s earnings momentum during the nine months ended 30 September 2026. Total operating income rose by 18.7% to Rs. 145.1 billion, from Rs. 122.2 billion in the corresponding period of the previous year, while net interest income increased by 21.5% to Rs. 126.2 billion from Rs. 103.9 billion. The bank also strengthened its Net Interest Margin (NIM) to 4.4% from 4.1%, supported by effective asset and liability repricing and disciplined balance sheet management. Together, these improvements highlight the strength of its core banking performance.

Sustained lending momentum was another key feature of the bank’s performance. Gross loans and advances reached Rs. 2.1 trillion, reflecting continued growth in core lending activities. At the same time, total assets stabilised at Rs. 3.9 trillion, demonstrating the bank’s ability to advance its lending business while maintaining overall balance sheet stability.

The bank’s improving capital strength provided further support for its growth momentum during the first nine months of 2026. Supported by sustained profitability and prudent balance sheet management, the Total Capital Adequacy Ratio rose to 17.4% as at 30 September 2026, from 16.5% at the end of 2025, remaining comfortably above the regulatory minimum requirements. Liquidity remained robust, with the Rupee Liquidity Coverage Ratio at 226.5%, reflecting substantial liquidity buffers and continued financial resilience.

Progress in asset quality complemented the bank’s loan portfolio expansion during the first nine months of 2026. The impaired loans (Stage 3) ratio (net) improved to 6.3%, while the Stage 3 provision coverage ratio strengthened to 54.1%. These improvements, achieved alongside continued loan portfolio growth, underscore enhanced recovery efforts, prudent credit risk management and the bank’s commitment to a resilient balance sheet.

People’s Bank’s strong performance momentum extended to the Group during the first nine months of 2026, supported by healthy core banking expansion and improved margins. Group PBT grew by 23.8% to Rs. 59.3 billion, compared with Rs. 47.9 billion in the corresponding period of the previous year, reflecting improved operating performance alongside disciplined cost and risk management.

The Group also sustained its business expansion, with gross loans and advances increasing to Rs. 2.4 trillion and total assets stabilising at Rs. 4.3 trillion. This performance reinforces the Group’s scale and business growth across key segments. Net interest income rose by 24.4% to Rs. 148.6 billion from Rs. 119.5 billion, supported by effective balance sheet repricing and sustained lending activity.

Improved profitability was further supported by a stronger Group Net Interest Margin, which increased to 4.8% from 4.4%, reflecting efficient asset-liability management and improved yields on interest-earning assets. The combined strength of earnings growth, business momentum and financial resilience further reinforces the Group’s strategic position as one of the country’s leading financial institutions.

Leadership Commentary

Chairman Chandana Guniyangoda highlighted People’s Bank’s continued resilience, financial strength and stability amid an evolving global and domestic economic environment. He observed that Sri Lanka’s economy has sustained its recovery momentum, supported by improved macroeconomic stability and growth across key sectors, even as geopolitical tensions, global uncertainties and emerging inflationary pressures continue to pose challenges.

The Chairman stressed that the bank’s performance is underpinned by a continued focus on stronger financial fundamentals, greater operational efficiency, sound governance and prudent risk management. He reaffirmed People’s Bank’s commitment to advancing national economic priorities by facilitating productive economic activity, supporting businesses and promoting financial inclusion, thereby contributing to sustainable and inclusive economic growth.

The CEO/General Manager Clive Fonseka described the bank’s performance as a demonstration of its sustained positive momentum, driven by robust core income generation, improved margins, stronger asset quality and a stable balance sheet. He emphasised that strong capital and liquidity positions, disciplined financial management and continued investments in digital banking, customer experience and operational efficiency position the bank well for sustainable growth.

Fonseka also drew attention to the bank’s achievement of the Overall Gold Award at the National Business Excellence Awards 2026, alongside top honours in the Extra-large, Local Market Reach and Banking Sector categories. He highlighted these accolades as recognition of the bank’s commitment to excellence in governance, innovation, customer service and overall business performance, as well as the dedication and professionalism of its employees. He reaffirmed the bank’s determination to build on this success, further strengthen its market position and deliver greater value to customers and stakeholders.

In recognition of the bank’s consistent and robust performance, Fitch Ratings recently upgraded People’s Bank’s National Long-Term Rating by two notches to AA+(lka), with a Stable Outlook. Following this upgrade, People’s Bank now shares the highest National Long-Term Rating among domestic commercial banks, placing it ahead of all private sector commercial banks in Sri Lanka on Fitch’s national rating scale and reaffirming its position among the country’s strongest and most trusted financial institutions.

The significance of this milestone is further underscored by the fact that this marks only the second occasion in the bank’s history that it has received a two-notch rating upgrade, with the first such upgrade having occurred in 2010.

title: Treasury moves to cut six months off project delays | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 05:05
-     - 8

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma – Pic by Upul Abayasekara

The Government has changed the way State institutions buy goods, works, and services. They can now complete most of the procurement process for next year’s projects before Parliament passes the Budget, a change the Treasury says will save six months in project delivery. The Treasury cited the reform as evidence that the State’s ability to deliver is improving, which analysts see as the main test of Budget 2027’s investment plan.

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma, speaking at the EY Sri Lanka Budget 2027 forum on 12 November, said procurement delays had long eaten into the time available to implement projects.

“Historically, we had to wait until the Budget was approved for the spending agencies, Government ministries, line agencies, and departments to start the procurement process,” Dr. Suriyapperuma said. “Some of the complex procurements and larger projects require at least six to eight months just to go through the procurement process. So, by the time you start the actual implementation, you are left with six months or less to implement.”

“That is why, historically, the ability to deliver was less,” he said.

He said the Treasury had proposed a new method to the National Procurement Commission (NPC), which accepted it. Institutions preparing 2027 projects can now advertise, call for tenders, shortlist bidders, appoint Bid Evaluation Committees (BECs) and High-Level Procurement Committees (HLPCs), and complete the whole process up to the point of award in the preceding year. Once Parliament approves the Budget, they can issue awards to the selected bidders from the first days of January.

“We have saved six months in the process to make sure projects are implemented as much as possible within the same period,” Dr. Suriyapperuma said.

The award itself must still wait for the Budget. Under the NPC’s Procurement Guidelines 2024, published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 2412/01 of 25 November 2024, an institution must ensure that budgetary provision is available before issuing a Letter of Acceptance to a winning bidder. It must then issue the letter within three working days of the award being approved and within the period the bid remains valid. The guidelines already require institutions to keep three-year Master Procurement Plans tied to the medium-term budgetary framework, submit annual procurement plans at the budgeting stage, and complete preparatory work well before bidding to reduce delays. HLPCs, which handle the largest contracts, and the BECs that assist them, are appointed by the Treasury Secretary.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said the State’s delivery record was already improving. He said the 2025 Budget was ready to implement from April 2025, leaving nine months, and Cyclone Ditwah took away the last month. “So, in reality, we had only eight months to deliver. Out of nearly Rs. 1.5 trillion, we were able to deliver approximately 80% within eight months,” he said. “That shows the ability of the Government to deliver is improving.”

“Obviously, there is room for us to improve further, but the ability to deliver is improving,” he said. “It is not by accident. It is by a curated strategy that we follow, monitoring closely, engaging stakeholders at all levels, and identifying ways to improve ourselves.”

Analysts have been more cautious. CT Smith said about 75% of the 2025 capital budget was spent. It said less than 30% of the 2026 capital budget, or about Rs. 385 billion of Rs. 1.38 trillion, had been spent in the first nine months. “Capital spending has a record of falling short of plan,” CT Smith said. Budget 2027 raises capital expenditure to Rs. 2 trillion, or 5.12% of GDP.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said the Treasury had also found ways to keep projects running beyond the 12-month Budget cycle. He said such projects had been constrained because Government budgeting is not on an accrual basis. Framework agreements, introduced last year, let institutions set up procurement tailored to their needs. “Instead of going through the standard procurement approaches, you can have dedicated, customised procurement arrangements for your institutions,” he said.

He said digitisation was the other lever, cutting the time taken to obtain approvals such as the bonded warehouses that power sector projects often need. He gave two examples.

The first was a VAT system introduced in 2025, which he said had been met with a lot of scepticism. He said it was rolled out after monthly meetings with chamber representatives and the Inland Revenue Department. “Every month on average, we get an extra Rs. 20 billion in collections. Plus or minus Rs. 10 billion goes as refunds back to the industry. So, we have a net positive of Rs. 10 billion a month,” he said, adding that this amounts to Rs. 120 billion a year. He said the law requires refunds within 45 days, but the system had made one refund in a single day because it reconciles automatically, without human intervention.

The second was the National Single Window for Trade, which went live on 5 November in pilot mode and is running alongside the manual process. “For 20 years, Sri Lanka tried to implement a single window for trade,” he said. Tea and coconut were the first two sectors onboarded. He said their first shipments went through a fully online process involving six agencies, including quarantine, standards, and Customs. The containers have already left Sri Lanka. Despite a technical glitch, he said, the clearances took no more than an hour or two. “That shows the system is working,” Dr. Suriyapperuma said.

He said the system cuts person-to-person contact, improves accuracy, and removes the opportunity for irregularities, sparing businesses the need to go from agency to agency for approvals. “The single window system that we are using is 100% built by local enterprises,” he said.

title: Seafood exporters hail Budget 2027, eye $ 680 m by 2030 | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 04:57
-     - 20

The Seafood Exporters’ Association of Sri Lanka (SEASL) yesterday said it “strongly supports” the Government’s 2027 Budget proposals, recognising their potential to accelerate investment, expand value-added seafood processing, strengthen sustainable fisheries and improve Sri Lanka’s international competitiveness.

The Association extends its appreciation to President and Finance, Planning and Economic Development Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake for recognising the strategic importance of the fisheries and seafood export industry. SEASL also thanks Fisheries, Aquatic and Ocean Resources Minister Ramalingam Chandrasekar and Deputy Minister Rathna Gamage for their commitment to developing the sector and supporting fishing communities.

SEASL believes Sri Lanka has the potential to achieve $ 680 million in annual seafood export earnings by 2030, provided the industry is supported by sustained investment, greater value addition, modern infrastructure and efficient trade policies.

The proposed concessionary financing scheme offering loans of up to Rs. 500 million at 5% annual interest to qualifying large-scale fisheries enterprises represents an important opportunity to accelerate investment in processing capacity, modern technology and cold-chain infrastructure.

The 200% enhanced capital allowance for qualifying BOI-approved export-oriented manufacturing investments of at least $ 3 million could further encourage expansion, new processing facilities and the development of higher-value seafood products.

These measures can help attract investment, strengthen Sri Lanka’s processing capabilities and create additional employment across the industry.

Sri Lanka’s seafood industry has demonstrated the considerable potential of value-added processing, particularly through the importation of raw materials for processing and re-export.

From January to September 2026, seafood exports generated $ 246.12 million, including $ 64 million from value-added products, representing 26% of total export earnings compared with just 4% in 2022.

This transformation highlights the importance of maintaining policies that enable Sri Lankan processors to source raw materials internationally, add value locally and supply global markets.

SEASL emphasises that continued access to imported raw materials for value addition is essential to sustaining factory utilisation, expanding employment and increasing foreign exchange earnings.

The proposed modernisation of the Temporary Importation for Export Processing (TIEP) scheme, customs digitalisation and the National Single Window for Trade should help simplify procedures, reduce costs and improve export competitiveness.

The Association supports the proposed Rs. 5 billion investment in Northern fisheries infrastructure, including Pesalai Harbour and fishery anchorages, which should improve landing facilities, product handling and livelihoods in coastal communities.

SEASL is particularly encouraged by the opportunities for Sri Lanka’s aquaculture farmers, who have the potential to play an increasingly important role in the development of the seafood export industry.

“We are excited about the opportunities ahead for our aquaculture farmers, particularly those engaged in shrimp farming. title: Athukorala’s Asian global production experiences: Lessons for Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 03:48
-     - 14

Drawing on rich historical evidence, Athukorala shows that the island has missed many opportunities, apart from its resilient garment and apparel industry which Athukorala says has benefitted from the transfer of technology and management skills

Even in retirement, an academic continues his journey

Professor Prema-chandra Athukorala, the Sri Lankan-born economist honoured by the Australian Government as a Member of the Order of Australia (AM) in 2026, has brought together his lifelong research on global production sharing, drawing on the experiences of some of Asia’s leading economies. 

In this new book, he devotes two important chapters to his country of birth, Sri Lanka. He recently retired as Professor of Economics at the Australian National University, which he fondly calls his "intellectual home", and the university has named him Professor Emeritus. Yet an academic of his standing rarely leaves intellectual life behind. From our past conversations, I know that he remains actively involved in research and doctoral supervision. When recently asked to write a foreword for a publication, he could not do so immediately because he was busy editing a student’s doctoral thesis. 

Athukorala continues to make Sri Lanka proud and stands alongside the island’s internationally renowned economists, such as Dr. Gamani Corea and Dr. Lal Jayawardena. His contribution to the field is clear: Google Scholar records well over 14,000 citations of his work, an achievement matched by very few contemporary economists.

Global production sharing networks or manufacturing value chains?

Athukorala’s latest book, Global Production Sharing, Industrialisation and Trade Patterns: Lessons and Insights from Asia, is published by World Scientific Publishing in Singapore. It contains 14 chapters, and the author acknowledges several co-authors who helped prepare the study. 

The title uses "global production sharing", a term coined by management guru Peter Drucker in 1985 to explain that modern manufactured goods are no longer products of a single nation but "products of the world". 

Athukorala focuses more specifically on the Global Manufacturing Value Chain (GMVC), as the book examines the physical manufacturing and assembly stages within these global networks. This focus makes the subject easier for ordinary readers to understand. It is also important because manufacturing has helped developing nations create industrial jobs, build wealth, and achieve prosperity. However, with the rise of artificial intelligence and advanced technology, a global services chain is also emerging. We may hope that, in his future work, Athukorala broadens his focus to a "global value chain plus" framework to cover these new digital developments.

Smiling Curve

Finding a place in the Global Manufacturing Value Chain (GMVC) is a complex task for any nation. It requires firm commitment from top policymakers, consistent long-term policies, quick action to solve problems, continued public support, and the ability to withstand external shocks caused by unpredictable global leaders. Success ultimately depends on the vision and leadership of the country’s top politicians. To illustrate this challenging journey, Athukorala introduces the "Smiling Curve", a concept originally proposed by Stan Shih, the founder of Taiwan’s Acer Corporation.

The Smiling Curve is a simple visual tool shaped like a smile. Economists use it to show how much value (or economic profit) is added at each stage of making a product. For developing nations, the discouraging feature is that value addition falls to its lowest level in the middle stage before rising again to complete the smile. 

The process starts at the top left with concept development and research and development (R&D), where value addition is highest. The curve slopes downwards as a country moves to product branding and design to meet market needs. It reaches its lowest point during physical manufacturing and assembly. This can discourage newcomers because the immediate financial rewards seem low.

However, the curve rises again as a country masters the stages on the right-hand side: distribution, marketing, final sales, and after-sales services. Every country must work its way along the curve to reach these more profitable stages. As Athukorala stresses, there is no shortcut to success. Nations must work hard and remain committed to climbing from the lowest point to the peak. Among the Asian nations reviewed in the book, Singapore, China, Malaysia, and Thailand stand out as clear winners, while newer entrants such as Indonesia, India, the Philippines, and Vietnam are moving rapidly towards success.

Sri Lanka’s missed opportunities except in the garment sector

But what about Sri Lanka? Drawing on rich historical evidence, Athukorala shows that the island has missed many opportunities, apart from its resilient garment and apparel industry which Athukorala says has benefitted from the transfer of technology and management skills. 

Although the overall story is disappointing, it also offers hope to policymakers seeking a fresh start. To use the door metaphor, a newcomer with a fresh approach may find it easier to open a completely closed door than one already jammed halfway. In my view, this is the starting point for Sri Lanka’s current administration which is committed to delivering a rich country and a beautiful life to people.

Although the overall story is disappointing, it also offers hope to policymakers seeking a fresh start. To use the door metaphor, a newcomer with a fresh approach may find it easier to open a completely closed door than one already jammed halfway. In my view, this is the starting point for Sri Lanka’s current administration which is committed to delivering a rich country and a beautiful life to people

China: From accommodation to discontent

In his analysis of China, a clear winner in global production sharing, Athukorala explains the country’s rapid rise as a leader in global production networks and its implications for ongoing US-China trade tensions. China is now a major global exporter whose importance cannot be ignored, even by its critics. 

The punitive tariffs imposed by US administration did not emerge overnight. In the early years, US policy favoured accommodating China as a development partner. As Athukorala notes, both major political parties in Washington agreed that integrating China into the global economy brought net gains to the US through lower consumer prices, more competitive companies, and greater opportunities for multilateral production—another term for global production networking. Although the influx of cheap Chinese exports created costs at home, American leaders believed these were temporary difficulties that would fade once the economy had adjusted.

However, this favourable view of bilateral trade broke down during the 2016 US presidential election. Mainstream economists such as Jagdish Bhagwati and Alan Blinder argued that American job losses were mainly caused by domestic automation and rapid productivity growth. Populist politicians, however, labelled the problem the "China Shock". 

During Donald Trump’s second administration, up to 2026, an open trade war erupted, with heated political rhetoric taking precedence over reasoned economic arguments. As the two superpowers imposed retaliatory tariffs on each other, the effects spread far beyond their borders, affecting countries across the global trading system.

Athukorala wrote this chapter just before the Trump camp suffered a heavy defeat in the US midterm elections in November 2026. Although the wider world hopes this political shift may help end the rivalry, an early settlement of the tariff war remains unlikely, given America’s longstanding commitment to putting "America First". Nevertheless, Athukorala closes the chapter on a reassuring note. He observes that other countries in global production networks specialise in distinct components, making them essential partners and helping to prevent the global trading system from collapsing.

Experiences of other Asian countries

In his case studies of Asian countries, Athukorala follows a clear structure: reviewing their history, assessing their current position, and offering concluding remarks. For ordinary readers, these conclusions bring together the book’s main lessons. Although the countries have taken different paths, their experiences offer a useful guide to development strategies.

Singapore stands out as a leading success story of the GMVC model. Its national development strategy centres on multinational enterprises (MNEs)—large companies that operate in several countries. Singapore which hosted these companies on its land has benefited greatly as these enterprises expanded their manufacturing operations into newly opened economies in Eastern Europe and Central Asia that had previously relied on central planning. These gains are particularly visible in the information and communications technology (ICT) sector.

In contrast, Indonesia’s uncertain policies and lack of consistent long-term direction have held back its economic transformation. Athukorala concludes: "Indonesia has so far failed to reap gains from the ongoing relocation production processes from China within GMVCs, particularly in the context of the US-China trade war." Although this is a harsh assessment, the same criticism applies to other developing nations that have failed to benefit from the shift of factories away from China amid global geopolitical tensions.

The Philippines has made limited progress despite joining global production networks early. Malaysia, by contrast, has been highly successful, with the Penang Export Hub playing a central role in its GMVC strategy. However, Athukorala warns that Malaysia must do more to sustain this success. It needs institutional reforms, targeted investment promotion, quick solutions to investors’ problems, world-class infrastructure, focused vocational training to develop a skilled workforce, and stronger links between multinational enterprises and local firms. Thailand has carved out a niche in the automotive industry, placing it in a strong position to enter the electric vehicle (EV) sector, which offers considerable potential for global growth.

Among the newer entrants, Vietnam has worked hard to join GMVCs by promoting foreign direct investment (FDI)—including investment by foreign companies in local factories—and strong export growth. These efforts have made Vietnam an important participant in global manufacturing. India, though a late entrant, is also making steady progress. It has developed growing automotive and electronics export sectors while moving away from the import substitution policies it followed for decades—the strategy of producing goods locally while restricting imports. 

Together, these Asian experiences show that, although the approaches differ, joining global networks can put economies on a path to prosperity. Athukorala does not say so directly, but this progress may signal the beginning of the "Asian Era" that regional political leaders often speak of.

Pathetic story of Sri Lanka

Athukorala’s two chapters on Sri Lanka are among the book’s most revealing and important sections for local readers. The country sought to industrialise as a way to overcome slow growth and severe unemployment. With the major economic shift in 1977, Sri Lanka began looking outward to global markets rather than inward. Yet inconsistent policies since then have held back a lasting transformation of its industrial structure.

Sri Lanka can fairly be described as a country of missed opportunities. It has repeatedly allowed promising global openings to slip away, with little apparent concern among its political leaders. Athukorala presents extensive evidence to support this disappointing account. He also notes that Sri Lanka is not alone: many developing nations have fallen into similar policy traps in the years since World War II.

Summing up his analysis of Sri Lanka, Athukorala offers a clear warning: "In sum, the analysis of regime shifts and economic performance under State-led import substitution strategy and liberalisation reforms in this paper makes a strong case for averting backsliding in policy, continuing the market-oriented reforms agenda that was left incomplete in the late 1990s, and setting up institutional safeguards to avert further policy backsliding."

Although Sri Lanka’s apparel sector benefited from technology transfer and the drive towards offshore investment in major importing countries in the 1970s and 1980s, the industry is now at a crossroads. Importing countries are increasingly looking to onshoring or nearshoring—bringing production home or closer to home—to reduce delays and costs through advanced automation and engineering technology. In this situation, although Athukorala does not spell it out in his chapter, Sri Lanka should develop its garment industry along GMVC principles. 

Rather than producing a whole garment, the country could focus on particular parts of the global value chain. This would require specialising in components and activities in which Sri Lanka has competitive and comparative advantages. One area that comes to mind is garment design using advanced AI and design technologies. In my view, Sri Lankans’ strong learning skills could help them master these technologies.

This is an important, non-partisan recommendation that Sri Lanka’s current administration should follow in both letter and spirit. To open the door to lasting prosperity, the country’s leaders must avoid short-sighted policy reversals, commit to long-term structural reforms, and establish legal and institutional safeguards to protect the economy from future political shifts.

Athukorala offers a bold and clear analysis of the economic challenges facing these Asian countries. His book not only explains past failures but also points to the steps they need to take next. It is a timely and valuable guide for developing nations, especially Sri Lanka, seeking lasting prosperity for their people. Athukorala has laid out the roadmap; it is now up to Sri Lanka’s policymakers to read it and act on its lessons

title: Sri Lanka’s energy policy  and the democratic dilemma | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 03:44
-     - 14

By protecting citizen-led rooftop solar  and investing in storage and grid modernisation, not only can the country reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels and move toward energy security but also drive the much-needed equal wealth distribution that the Government touts is the foundation of prosperity. Not only the elected officials, but we, the public, also have a responsibility to ensure that administrative institutions implement democratic policy for the good of the country rather than obstructing it with ulterior motives

By Prof. Emeritus I. M. Dharmadasa, Brig. Ranjan de Silva, Eng. Vidhura Ralapanawe, and Dr. Geewananda Gunawardane

Democratic governments depend on a professional civil service to turn laws and policy goals into sustained public action. Because bureaucrats exercise substantial influence without being directly accountable to voters, tension can arise when administrative decisions diverge from elected priorities or the public interest, a problem often described as the “democratic dilemma”. Sri Lanka’s electricity sector provides a consequential example, particularly in the treatment of renewable energy and citizen-funded rooftop solar.

Drawing on four decades of experience in renewable-energy research and commercialisation, we offer these observations to the President and the public in the hope that Sri Lanka can resolve the democratic dilemma in favor of economic and social progress. A capable bureaucracy is essential to maintaining beneficial policies through frequent changes in political leadership. Sri Lanka has a clear path to energy independence, the foundation of the prosperity this Government promised, yet bureaucratic obstruction continues to slow progress. This article examines whether that failure arises from gaps in knowledge, institutional capacity, or accountability, and what must change to protect the public interest.

Three decades of resistance to renewables

While researching solar-energy conversion in UK academia and working on solar commercialisation at the British Petroleum Company, one author, IMD, concluded that the technology was mature enough to support social development. As a professor at Sheffield Hallam University, he secured funding from the UK Department for International Development to establish a Higher Education Link (HE-Link) with Sri Lanka. Launched in 1992, the program brought together the universities of Peradeniya, Colombo, Moratuwa, Kelaniya, Jaffna, and Ruhuna along with relevant industries. The British Council managed the project, while IMD coordinated it for six years and facilitated more than 35 visits by senior academics between Sri Lanka and the UK. Its goals were to strengthen collaboration among Sri Lankan universities in solar-energy research, promote clean energy for sustainable development, reduce poverty, translate political freedom, however belatedly, into economic freedom, and mitigate climate change.

During the program’s six years, the British Council, the British High Commission in Colombo, and the Ministry of Science and Technology organised high-profile conferences. IMD also promoted renewable energy directly with nearly every science and technology minister from Bernard Soysa onward, as well as two former presidents. From 2002 to 2004, while Milinda Moragoda served as Minister of Economic Reform, Science and Technology, IMD joined an expatriate scientist exchange program to advance solar-energy research and development. The collaboration involved the ministry, the Ceylon Institute of Scientific and Industrial Research (now ITI), the National Engineering Research and Development (NERD) Centre, and Sri Lankan universities.

Institutional resistance to solar-energy development emerged during these high-level discussions. At one conference, the consortium invited the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) to present its national energy plans. Senior policymaker Shavi Fernando delivered a PowerPoint presentation whose concluding slide, projecting rapidly increasing demand, stated: “The future of Sri Lanka is coal, coal, and coal.” 

Dr Tilak Siyambalapitiya, later Chairman of CEB, also expressed opposition to renewables on many occasions. Our esteemed academic and industrial consortium members found these positions troubling because available scientific evidence indicated that Sri Lanka could achieve energy independence by properly developing its natural resources. In the authors’ view, the Energy Circular PE/DEV/03/01-RT, issued on 11 September 2026, shows that this “democratic dilemma” persists despite the current Government’s stated intentions and its structural and personnel changes.

Rise of rooftop solar and recent setbacks

Despite successive governments’ limited promotion of solar energy, the introduction of Soorya Bala Sangramaya in 2016 marked an important advance. Its net-metering, net-accounting, net-plus, and net-plus-plus schemes enabled entrepreneurs and households to expand rooftop generation. According to the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka’s (PUCSL) December 2025 report, the country had 129,300 to 150,000 rooftop solar connections, representing about 1940 MW to 2,090 MW of installed capacity. Nearly 1,000 solar photovoltaic companies now support about 40,000 skilled jobs. Notably, this expansion was financed by private citizens rather than the Government.

We welcome the current Government’s support for battery installation, an approach the CEB neglected for three decades. Batteries can store surplus daytime solar generation for nighttime use, reducing reliance on exceptionally costly diesel power. The Cabinet’s approval of a $ 35 million ADB financing package for a nationwide rooftop-solar project is also encouraging. These initiatives should be aligned with policies that preserve, rather than restrict, citizen participation in rooftop generation.

The 2025 PUCSL report identifies practical measures for integrating more rooftop solar, including formal connection standards, improved monitoring, advanced inverter functions, and battery storage. The following excerpt shows that the regulator treats higher distributed generation as a challenge to be managed through technical rules and grid visibility, rather than as a reason to halt rooftop-solar expansion:

“As rooftop solar penetration grows, utilities must be guided by formalised grid connection codes and operational guidelines that define the minimum technical and service requirements for connecting rooftop systems. These should include standardised inverter settings, metering configurations, voltage regulation practices, feeder hosting capacity assessment procedures, and time-bound service delivery commitments. Establishing and enforcing such utility-level requirements will help reduce consumer complaints, minimise operational issues such as inverter tripping and voltage rise, and improve the overall quality and performance of rooftop systems. 

Furthermore, as distributed generation continues to expand, improving real-time visibility and controllability of rooftop PV systems will be essential for national system stability. The integration of battery storage, advanced inverter functions, and monitoring systems will support this transition by enabling better management of mid-day surplus generation and reducing the operational burden on the national grid.”

Many CEB engineers support renewable energy, yet senior decision makers appear to discount their views while continuing to favor imported, polluting fossil fuels. Without transparent, evidence-based explanations, this pattern suggests that longstanding bureaucratic resistance persists despite restructuring and personnel changes, the “democratic dilemma” in practice. Authorities commonly argue that accommodating more rooftop solar would require a $ 4-5 billion grid upgrade taking 7–12 years or longer. Because the basis and alternatives behind that estimate have not been publicly explained here, it should be independently examined rather than treated as conclusive.

Public conundrum

When a people’s Government elected on the platform of taking power away from the entrenched elite and ensuring public good acts against its own policies, it becomes a grave concern for all. The Government’s actions appear inconsistent with its stated energy policies. Citizens are told that the grid cannot accommodate rooftop-generated electricity, while large corporate solar projects are supported on environmentally sensitive land and bodies of water. Taxes remain high on small-capacity batteries but have been completely removed for batteries used in large storage facilities. These choices raise three questions that require clear public answers: What technical and economic evidence justifies different treatment for household and large-scale projects? How will policy protect citizens who financed much of the country’s rooftop solar capacity? And does the 11 September 2026 circular shift control and economic benefits from distributed public generation toward corporate entities or monopolies?

The same policy choices also affect Sri Lanka’s ability to meet Sustainable Development Goal 7. The Sri Lanka SDG Report 2024 states that renewable energy’s share of total final energy consumption remains below the country’s 2030 ambition. Restricting distributed solar while delaying the phase-out of fossil fuels therefore risks widening the gap between national commitments and actual progress. In simple terms, the Government’s actions do not make any technical or political sense.

Unless the Government justifies its actions and discloses the evidence behind its decisions, the public cannot determine whether current policy reflects sound technical judgment or undue bureaucratic influence. Elected officials cannot be experts in every field; they depend on a professional civil service to provide accurate advice and implement policy in the public interest. The pressing issue is if the current Policy Advisory Committee is capable of providing such guidance. Based on their prior associations with the CEB hierarchy, and their policy directives, we have reason to conclude that four out of the five members are inclined to continue to support the said “The future of Sri Lanka is coal, coal, and coal” policy. When that process lacks transparency or accountability, and is not supported by data, citizens have a duty to demand evidence, oversight, and corrective action.

Sri Lanka already possesses substantial renewable resources and technical expertise; its energy future now depends on whether public institutions use them transparently, consistently, and in the national interest. By protecting citizen-led rooftop solar and investing in storage and grid modernisation, not only can the country reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels and move toward energy security but also drive the much-needed equal wealth distribution that the Government touts is the foundation of prosperity. Not only the elected officials, but we, the public, also have a responsibility to ensure that administrative institutions implement democratic policy for the good of the country rather than obstructing it with ulterior motives.

Water is how most people first experience climate change. Whether through prolonged drought, devastating floods or increasingly unpredictable rainfall, its effects reach directly into people’s lives, threatening food production, livelihoods, public health and economic security

For three decades, the international response to climate change has focused on reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The energy transition has become central to this effort, shaping national policies, mobilising investment and driving innovation. Now, as the world confronts the consequences of climate change already under way, we must give water the same prominence in our approach to adaptation.

Water is how most people first experience climate change. Whether through prolonged drought, devastating floods or increasingly unpredictable rainfall, its effects reach directly into people’s lives, threatening food production, livelihoods, public health and economic security. 

So, if energy has been the defining concern of climate mitigation, water must become the defining concern of adaptation, and to be effective, recognition must be matched by resources. Water already features in the national climate plans of most countries and is the sector most frequently identified in their adaptation measures. Yet inclusion in a national plan is not the same as meaningful action. Investment remains insufficient, fragmented and poorly coordinated.

The scale of the shortfall is considerable. The World Bank estimates that closing the annual financing gap for universal access to safe drinking water and sanitation requires between 

$ 131 billion and $ 141 billion. Behind this figure are communities without reliable drinking water, children exposed to preventable disease and populations whose livelihoods and security are threatened by drought and flooding.

Leaders must close the gap between their commitments and the resources allocated to deliver them. Water infrastructure, sanitation and resilient water management cannot remain underfunded priorities in national adaptation strategies. They require sustained investment, clear accountability and political leadership capable of translating plans into tangible improvements in people’s lives.

There are encouraging examples of the leadership required. The Madrid Compact, endorsed by 30 governments, offers a framework for stronger political commitment, integrated policies, sustainable financing and accountability. The Heads of State Initiative, supported by Sanitation and Water for All, has demonstrated how national leadership can translate commitments on water and sanitation into action. These approaches deserve wider application.

The same determination is needed internationally. Water connects the three Rio Conventions, addressing climate change, biodiversity loss and land degradation. Yet their respective work does not always reflect the interconnected nature of these challenges, or the central role water plays across all three.

COP31 offers an opportunity to change this. I call on world leaders to give water a stronger and more systematic place across the Rio Conventions, ensuring that their policies, programmes and investments are better aligned. This does not require new institutions or additional bureaucracy. It requires greater coordination through the structures we already have, with water recognised as a shared priority rather than an issue confined to individual policy discussions.

Leaders must close the gap between their commitments and the resources allocated to deliver them. Water infrastructure, sanitation and resilient water management cannot remain underfunded priorities in national adaptation strategies. They require sustained investment, clear accountability and political leadership capable of translating plans into tangible improvements in people’s lives

This commitment should then be carried forward to the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi in December, co-hosted by the UAE and Senegal. The conference provides an important opportunity to turn the political momentum generated at COP31 into a more coherent international approach, with water firmly embedded in the global response to interconnected environmental challenges.

We cannot afford to treat adaptation as secondary to mitigation, or water as secondary to adaptation. Leaders must recognise water as fundamental to the security, prosperity and wellbeing of their people, to match their commitments with the necessary investment, and to work together across the Rio Conventions.

The decisions made at COP31 and carried forward to Abu Dhabi can help establish the political foundations for a more water-secure future. What is needed now is the determination to act.
