title: Investing in Sri Lanka’s resilience: The case for patient capital | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 03:06
-     - 15

Whenever economies emerge from turbulent periods, recovery narratives are almost always framed through macroeconomic scorecards such as foreign exchange reserves, currency stabilisations, and sovereign credit trajectories. When Fitch Ratings upgraded Sri Lanka’s sovereign rating to 'B-' with a Stable Outlook was one encouraging sign. Tourist arrivals  reaching 1.64 million visitors in late 2026 nearly offered another indication of recovery, although challenges remained. 

Yet for international investors, recovery presents a deeper question of purpose. Some investors enter emerging markets when valuations are low, seeking quick returns, and preparing to leave at the first hint of volatility. 

That approach fundamentally misunderstands how resilient economies are built. Sustainable recovery requires more than capital seeking a quick return. It requires patient capital, a willingness to invest across economic cycles, develop people’s skills, and stay committed through difficult periods.

Commitment across economic cycles 

Enduring commercial value is created through resilience, not retreat. When a host nation faces external shocks, the conventional corporate playbook advises retrenchment by halting capital expenditure, cutting payrolls, and mothballing operational assets until complete certainty returns. 

The approach must be to continue investing through those difficult periods. For example, our hospitality arm Asia Leisure, chose to maintain and upgrade boutique properties such as Le Grand Galle, The Habitat Kosgoda, and Tamarind Hill through the most challenging seasons of recent years. Rather than scaling back, we focused on continuous property enhancements, service refinement, and operational readiness. 

This was not speculative optimism, but a recognition that tourism infrastructure cannot simply be switched off and restarted when conditions improve. When properties are preserved and revitalised during downturns, they are better placed to welcome visitors when demand returns. 

Continuing to invest also demonstrates confidence in Sri Lanka’s future and a commitment to an enduring partnership.

Hospitality’s wider economic contribution

 Nowhere is the compounding power of patient capital clearer than in hospitality. As Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya recently emphasised, achieving Sri Lanka's 2030 tourism ambitions requires more than physical infrastructure development. It demands a skilled workforce, quality employment generation, and the active empowerment of youth and women. 

Far from a purely recreational sector, tourism operates as an essential economic catalyst, directly driving national employment and ensuring that the benefits of growth reach regional communities. 

There is an outdated assumption that commercial returns and community welfare exist in conflict, as if generating shareholder value requires minimising local expenditure. In truth, sustainable commercial success and local economic prosperity reinforce each other. A hotel’s long-term success is closely tied to the wellbeing of the community around it. Its long-term viability depends on the vitality, skill, and goodwill of that community. 

In coastal hubs like Galle and Kosgoda, we have  always placed importance on developing local talent. By recruiting locally, providing continuous vocational training, and developing career pathways for young men and women, commercial investment helps families build more secure livelihoods. The benefits extend to local businesses through sourcing produce from local farmers, partnering with artisanal fishermen, contracting regional transport operators, and engaging neighbourhood craftsmen. When an investor deliberately roots their supply chain in the domestic community, commercial growth creates opportunities well beyond the hotel itself.

An ASEAN investor’s perspective on Sri Lanka’s potential

 Viewing Sri Lanka through the lens of Southeast Asia’s economic journey reveals striking parallels. Over three decades, ASEAN economies navigated repeated financial crises, geopolitical shifts, and external shocks. What propelled the region into one of the world's most vibrant economic blocs was not the absence of shocks, but the resilience of private enterprise and the steady inflow of patient capital that looked past short-term headlines. 

Sri Lanka possesses important strengths, including an educated and adaptable workforce, an extraordinary cultural and ecological heritage, and a strategic geographic position in the Indian Ocean.  For long-term investors, periods of volatility do not erase that potential. 

By committing early and demonstrating staying power, international investors do more than generate financial returns. Their continued investment can give others greater confidence in Sri Lanka’s long-term potential and encourage them to explore opportunities of their own.

The value of continuous reinvestment 

National resilience is ultimately built over decades, not measured in quarterly earnings. 

Governments establish the policy frameworks and monetary conditions for recovery, but private capital must breathe life into the real economy. When businesses reject the easy exit and choose instead to reinvest in people, preserve physical infrastructure, and uplift regional communities, they cease to be foreign entities observing from the margins. They become genuine stakeholders in the country's collective future. 

Sri Lanka has repeatedly demonstrated an extraordinary capacity to endure and rebuild. For those of us who have stayed the course, our conviction is clear, the future of this nation belongs to those who have the patience to build alongside it.

(The author is Executive Chairman of the QI Group of Companies)

title: Budget 2027: The proof  of the pudding is in the execution | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 02:58
-     - 16

The intent is progressive. But for three years running, Sri Lanka has budgeted far more for development than it has managed to spend. Is the problem the estimates, or the machinery that is meant to deliver them?

The 2027 Budget, presented on 12 November, reads well. Its stated aim is to strengthen the production economy, protect small and medium industrialists, make room for investment, connect technology to the economy, protect the environment and ensure social justice. It does this while keeping to the fiscal discipline the country has painfully rebuilt since 2022.

I have no quarrel with the intent. It is progressive, and in several areas it is genuinely bold. But budgets are not judged by their speeches. They are judged by what is built, paid for and delivered by the following December. And on that measure, the record of the last two budgets should give us pause.

What the Budget gets right

There is a great deal to welcome:

income tax relief rises from Rs. 1.8 million to Rs. 1.95 million a year, the tax bands are revised, and Rs. 230 billion goes to social protection, including Aswesuma.

enterprises, a Public-Private Partnership Act, a Digital Economy Bill and a review of labour laws.

If all of this is delivered, 2027 could be the year Sri Lanka moves beyond stabilisation to growth. The word that matters in that sentence is “delivered.”

The execution gap

Here is the uncomfortable truth. For three consecutive years, the State has allocated far more for capital investment than it has spent.

Against this record, the 2027 Budget raises the capital allocation to Rs. 2,000 billion, 45% more than the 2026 allocation, and more than five times what had been spent in the first nine months of this year. The Government says most capital spending traditionally happens in the final quarter. That may be so. But that is precisely the problem: money rushed out of the door in November and December is rarely money well spent.

Unrealistic estimates, or a machine that cannot deliver?

The question every reader should ask is why. I see two possible explanations, and the evidence suggests both are at work.

The first is that the estimates are unrealistic. Budgets in Sri Lanka have long served two purposes: as financial plans and as political statements. A large capital allocation signals ambition, even when the projects behind it are not ready. The 2024 estimates assumed that debt restructuring would be completed early and that halted foreign-funded projects would restart quickly. Neither happened in time. An IMF assessment found that only a third of major projects had feasibility studies, and that more than half entered the budget without proper appraisal. When projects are funded before they are ready, under-spending is not an accident. It is built into the budget.

The second is that the line ministries lack the capacity to deliver. The World Bank is explicit on this point. It says the under-execution “reflects weaknesses in public investment management, including project selection, procurement, and implementation capacity,” and not a shortage of finance. That matters. With revenue running ahead of target, money is no longer the binding constraint. The machinery is.

The Citizens Budget itself gives a telling picture of that machinery. The public service employs over 225,000 teachers and more than 100,000 development officers. But its cadre table lists just 1,138 officers in the Sri Lanka Engineers’ Service, 802 in the Planning Service, 1,611 Sri Lanka Accountants and 55 architects. Other technical staff sit in agencies and state enterprises, but this core cadre is the one that plans, procures, supervises and pays for the roads, water schemes and canals the Budget promises. Rs. 2,000 billion of capital investment rests on a remarkably thin layer of technical capacity.

Add to this outdated procurement rules, land acquisition delays, weak coordination between agencies and the long-standing habit of starting more projects than can be finished, and the pattern becomes clear.

There is also a third, less discussed factor. In an environment of heightened scrutiny, which the country rightly demanded after 2022, many public officials have become reluctant to sign. Delay carries no personal risk; a decision that is later questioned does. Accountability is essential, but when it is not matched by clear rules and protection for honest decisions made in good faith, the safest course for an official is to do nothing. The result is a public service that is clean but slow.

Why under-spending is not a saving

Some will argue that unspent money is money saved. It is not.

A Budget has vision and strategy. Execution needs system, structure competency

In my work with organisations, I often use a simple framework. Vision is where we are going. Strategy is how we will get there. But neither delivers anything without a system, the processes, measures and incentives through which work actually gets done, and a structure that makes clear who owns what.

Budget 2027 has a clear vision and, in most areas, sensible choices. What it does not yet have is a delivery system and a structure of accountability strong enough to carry Rs. 2,000 billion of investment. That is where the Government's attention must now turn.

What India does differently

On 1 February this year, India’s Finance Minister presented a Budget for 1.45 billion people in 85 minutes. India is at a very different stage, with an economy many times our size and no recent default to recover from. Its capital program of about ₹12.2 trillion, roughly $ 130 billion, is beyond anything we can contemplate. But the lesson that matters is not the size of its Budget. It is the delivery.

The usual comparisons between the two budgets mislead more than they inform. Set side by side in dollars, India’s Budget dwarfs ours, and some have even claimed that Sri Lanka spends more per citizen. That ignores the fact that India’s Union Budget covers only its Central Government, while its states run most health, education and policing from their own budgets. The fairer comparison is in ratios, and there the two countries look surprisingly alike. India’s Central Government plans a fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP; ours is 4.5%. India spends 26% of its Budget on interest; we spend about a third. Interest absorbs about 40% of India’s central revenue and about 43% of ours. Where the two countries part company is in what happens after the Budget is passed.

In 2024-25, India’s Central Government spent about 95% of its original capital budget, against about 75% in Sri Lanka in 2025. In 2025-26, it spent about ₹10.75 trillion, 98% of its revised target, as reported by Construction World citing a senior official. Sri Lanka, by contrast, had spent less than 30% of its 2026 capital allocation by the end of September.

Part of the difference lies in a discipline India has built into its Budget process. Since 2017, every major central scheme has been published with an Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework: about 400 schemes and nearly 4,000 indicators, tracked on a public dashboard and tabled in Parliament with the Budget. This is accountability demonstrated. Under India’s General Financial Rules, a scheme’s performance against those targets helps decide whether it continues and how much it receives the following year. In other words, ministries are funded for outcomes, not just for intentions.

India is not perfect. Its states, which build much of its infrastructure, struggle with capital spending too. But at the centre, it has made one thing clear: an allocation is a promise, and promises are tracked.

What must change

1. Fund only projects that are ready. No major project should enter the budget without a completed feasibility study, appraisal, land and approvals in place. Projects that are not ready should be funded for preparation, not construction.

2. Budget for outcomes and publish execution every quarter. As India does with its Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework, each ministry’s allocation should come with measurable outputs and outcomes. Parliament’s Committee on Public Finance and the public should see allocation, spending and project milestones every quarter, and next year’s allocation should depend on this year’s delivery. What gets measured and published gets managed.

3. Create a delivery unit with real authority. A small, highly skilled unit of professionals under the President, of the kind Malaysia used to drive its transformation program, should track the top 50 projects, unblock bottlenecks across ministries and report progress openly.

4. Fix procurement. Expand e-procurement, update the Administrative and Financial Regulations, set fixed timelines for each procurement stage, and delegate authority to the level where decisions can be made quickly.

5. Buy in the capacity we lack. Engage engineers, quantity surveyors and project managers on contract, use the new PPP framework, and draw on private-sector project management where the state lacks skills.

6. Protect honest decisions. Officials who follow due process and act in good faith must be protected when outcomes are later questioned. Accountability should target corruption and negligence, not judgement.

7. Budget on a realistic baseline. Start each year's capital allocation from what was actually delivered the year before, plus a credible pipeline of ready projects. Ambition should be shown in delivery, not in the size of the allocation.

The real test

This Government came to office on a promise of a different kind of governance, and its fiscal management has earned genuine credit. Revenue is up, the deficit is under control, and the country is emerging from the IMF program in March 2027 in far better shape than it entered it.

But the next phase is harder. Stabilisation was largely about saying no: to waste, to new taxes on the wrong people, to unfunded promises. Growth is about saying yes, and then delivering. The President's aspirations can only be realised through ministries, departments and officials who have the competency, the systems and the confidence to act.

The pudding has been well described. By 31 December 2027, we will know whether it was cooked.

(The author is a former Senior Banker, Regional Director of CIMA for the Middle East, South Asia and North Africa, Head Of PPP (2017) and has served on two national Education Reform Commissions. He is the Founder of Business Athletes and Teen Academy)

A late second-half strike enabled Pakistan to edge past hosts Bangladesh 1-0 and shatter their hopes of reaching the final in a fiercely contested semi-final of the 15th SAFF Football Championship played under floodlights at the National Stadium in Dhaka, Bangladesh, on Saturday.

It was a heartbreaking finish for the home side, who came agonisingly close to forcing their way into the grand finale, only to be undone by a clinical Pakistan outfit in the dying stages of the game. Pakistan finally broke the deadlock in the 86th minute, with the solitary goal proving decisive and sealing their place in tomorrow’s (17) final at the same venue.

The much-anticipated semi-final lived up to its billing, with both sides producing an entertaining contest marked by high intensity, tactical discipline, and attacking intent.

Bangladesh, buoyed by their emphatic 4-0 victory over Sri Lanka, entered the contest as favourites, backed by a vociferous home crowd that packed the stadium, waving banners and passionately cheering their beloved Bangali Tigers.

Skipper Hamza Choudhary and Farhan Ali, two overseas-based players from London, were the focal points of Bangladesh’s attacking game, with the home side banking heavily on their creativity and ability to unlock the opposition defence through incisive passing and attacking combinations.

However, the Pakistan technical bench had clearly studied their opponents well and executed a tactical game plan to neutralise the threat posed by Bangladesh’s key playmakers. Their defensive organisation and disciplined marking restricted the hosts from exploiting spaces in the final third.

Bangladesh enjoyed a few promising attacking spells and carved out some scoring opportunities, but their finishing lacked the cutting edge required at this crucial stage of the competition. Despite enjoying periods of possession and pushing forward in search of the breakthrough, they failed to find the back of the net.

With the deadlock remaining unbroken, both teams stepped up the tempo after the interval, as the contest developed into an end-to-end battle, with neither side willing to surrender territorial advantage.

Pakistan, who had shown considerable improvement following their closely fought 3-2 encounter against their traditional rivals in the curtain-raiser, began to dictate the attacking exchanges. Their forwards pressed high up the pitch, putting the Bangladesh backline under mounting pressure and forcing the home defenders into some anxious moments.

The decisive breakthrough came in the 86th minute when Pakistan striker Abdul Samad Arshad capitalised on a well-timed delivery from the midfield. Showing excellent ball control and attacking awareness, he split two Bangladesh defenders before unleashing a fierce left-footed drive that beat the goalkeeper and found the back of the net.

The late goal stunned the home crowd and left Bangladesh with little time to mount a meaningful comeback.

The closing minutes witnessed Bangladesh throwing men forward in a desperate attempt to restore parity, while Pakistan dropped deeper, tightened their defensive net, and protected their slender lead with determination. The visitors successfully weathered the late onslaught to emerge victorious and book their place in the final.

With this memorable semi-final triumph, Pakistan will now face traditional rivals India in tomorrow’s much-anticipated championship decider.

Earlier, India also had to dig deep to overcome Bhutan 2-1 in the other semi-final, booking their place in the final and setting up a mouth-watering showdown against Pakistan.

India will now be targeting their 10th SAFF Championship crown when the two regional football powerhouses lock horns in what promises to be a thrilling finale.

Padel House has invested in an integrated sports and lifestyle complex at the Ceylonese Rugby and Football Club (CR&FC), with Padel House Co-founder Shamal Perera confirming the combined investment of Rs. 175 million at its launch last evening. 

The company seeks to capitalise on growing interest in padel and emerging commercial opportunities across the sports, wellness and recreation sectors.

The facility goes beyond conventional court-based sports, combining padel with fitness, wellness, hospitality and family-oriented activities.

The CR&FC venue now has four courts, up from two, as well as a café by Crust and Crumble, a children’s play area by Sensory Station, a Pilates studio by Barressential and nail and spa services by Gloe. The Recovery Room provides additional recovery and wellness facilities, including services for both professional athletes and recreational users.

“The complex is designed to cater to players and non-playing family members through its range of dining, fitness, wellness and recreational services. We believe this will be more than just a padel court or a café. It will be a lifestyle centre that everyone will enjoy,” Perera said.

Trade Promoters Ltd. Australasia’s girls had earlier posted 155 for seven, thanks largely to Lexie McLeavy Cantrill’s sparkling 82 off 48 deliveries, an innings studded with six sixes and five boundaries.

However, Kanchan turned the contest on its head with a devastating spell before returning to anchor the reply as Sub-Saharan Africa reached 171 for five.

Australasia’s boys then threatened to wrest back the initiative, with Vansh Gemini launching a blistering assault. His 85 off just 39 balls, featuring seven sixes, propelled his side to 195 all out.

Kanchan was deservedly named Player of the Match.

The historic encounter provided an encouraging beginning for Test Twenty, where boys’ and girls’ teams contribute towards a combined result rather than competing for separate honours.

Under the tournament’s Parity Rule, performances from both XIs carry equal weight, ensuring victory is genuinely a collective effort.

title: A 4-0 defeat and storm of controversy: Sri Lanka Football deserves answers | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 16 November 2026 03:02
-     - 9

By Hishan Welimilla

Sri Lanka’s 4-0 defeat to Bangladesh was disappointing enough. But what followed the match has raised even more serious questions about the state of football administration in South Asia, the transparency of the regional governing body, and the future of Sri Lankan football.

The controversial remarks made by Sri Lanka Head Coach Abdullah Al Mutairi at the post-match press conference have brought an entirely different dimension to the situation.

His allegations against the South Asian Football Federation (SAFF) raise important questions about fairness, accountability, and the treatment of coaches within the regional football structure.

A mysterious midnight email before the match

According to Al Mutairi, he received an email from the SAFF around midnight on the eve of the match, demanding an explanation within just 10 hours. He claimed that the communication threatened him with a six-month suspension and a fine of $ 10,000 if he failed to respond within the stipulated period.

If these allegations are accurate, serious questions must be asked.

Is it appropriate for a regional governing body to issue such a demanding disciplinary communication just hours before an important international fixture? Could such an intervention affect a coach’s mental preparation and, indirectly, the team’s performance?

The issue is not simply whether a disciplinary complaint existed, but whether the procedure followed was fair, transparent, and consistent with established regulations.

Are Arab coaches being treated differently?

Al Mutairi has made an even more serious allegation, claiming that Arab coaches and nationals face discrimination and double standards within the SAFF.

He also referred to his experience in 2021, when he guided Nepal to the SAFF Championship final, claiming that he encountered similar unfair treatment during that campaign.

These are serious allegations that cannot simply be dismissed as emotional reactions following a disappointing result.

However, allegations alone are not proof. They must be examined through an independent and transparent investigation. The SAFF must have an opportunity to respond, while Al Mutairi should provide the evidence he says is in his possession.

What does this mean for Sri Lankan football?

Perhaps the most unfortunate aspect of this controversy is that the team’s actual performance against Bangladesh risks being overshadowed by the dispute between the Coach and the regional governing body.

A 4-0 defeat demands serious questions about Sri Lanka’s football development and the team’s preparation.

Why did Sri Lanka’s game plan fail so comprehensively?

Why was the defensive structure so vulnerable?

Were the coach’s tactical decisions appropriate for the opposition?

Did the players execute the required game plan?

What responsibility should the football administration take for the team’s continuing struggles?

These questions deserve proper answers. It would be unfortunate if the entire discussion surrounding Sri Lankan football became centred on a controversy with the SAFF while the fundamental problems affecting the national team remained unaddressed.

“I will never return to SAFF region”

Al Mutairi has reportedly declared that he will never again coach in the SAFF region. He has also indicated that he intends to make public the evidence and email correspondence he claims to possess.

That is ultimately his personal decision. However, for a country such as Sri Lanka, which is attempting to rebuild its position in international football, the consequences of this controversy cannot be ignored.

The future of the national team should not become collateral damage in a personal or administrative dispute.

At the same time, if a coach representing Sri Lanka has been subjected to unfair treatment, the country’s football authorities have a responsibility to seek clarification and demand accountability.

Silence cannot be the answer.

What Sri Lankan Football needs now is accountability, not excuses

The SAFF must respond officially to the allegations. Al Mutairi must provide the evidence he has promised to disclose. The Sri Lanka Football Federation must also explain its position and clarify what steps, if any, it has taken to address the matter.

But above everything else, Sri Lankan football needs to confront its sporting failures.

What the country needs is not a coach engaged in endless disputes with SAFF, but a coach capable of taking the national team towards international success. Similarly, Sri Lanka needs football administrators who accept responsibility for defeats, address structural weaknesses, and work towards rebuilding the game rather than relying on excuses and promises.

Ultimately, the 4-0 defeat to Bangladesh should serve as a wake-up call.

The controversy surrounding Al Mutairi may eventually fade, but the problems confronting Sri Lankan football will remain unless decisive action is taken.

Sri Lankan football needs more than promises. It needs answers, accountability and meaningful change.

Gamer.LK’s Play Expo 2026, powered by Maggi Papare Blast, is ready to welcome the country’s best Esports talent and fandom on 5 and 6 December at the Sri Lanka Exhibition and Convention Centre (SLECC). 

Registrations are currently underway for over 30 tournaments across 23 titles spanning PC, mobile, console, simulator, and Virtual Reality (VR). With roots that go all the way back to the Sri Lanka Cyber Games, which began in 2008, the event has been attracting gamers and gaming enthusiasts for almost two decades.

Team tournaments feature Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, League of Legends, Overwatch, Rainbow Six Siege, Valorant and Call of Duty 4 on PC, alongside PUBG MOBILE, Free Fire, Mobile Legends, Call of Duty Mobile and Honor of Kings, on mobile. Individual players can compete in Mortal Kombat 1, Street Fighter VI, Tekken 8 and eFootball on PC; Clash Royale, eFootball on mobile; FC 27 on console; the F1 26 Simulator; and Beat Saber in VR.

The Women’s Championship returns with Free Fire, League of Legends, Mobile Legends, Mortal Kombat 1, PUBG MOBILE and Valorant, while the Kids Championship features Subway Surfers and Temple Run for players aged 12 and below.

Play Expo 2026 has been recognised as a ranked tournament by the Sri Lanka Esports Association (SLESA), the governing body for Esports in Sri Lanka. Results from the ranked titles will count towards the official national player rankings, giving local players the chance to be considered for the national Esports team.

Gamer.LK CEO Raveen Wijayatilake said: “Play Expo is the focal point for Esports in Sri Lanka every year. It’s where we watch brand new talent flourish and then go on to represent the country in tournaments the world over. It’s been especially rewarding to see women’s Esports grow, with more women competing every year. Since Sri Lanka Cyber Games began in 2008, Sri Lankan gaming has grown from a hobby into a national sport – and this is our biggest line-up of tournaments yet. Above all, Play Expo is a space for the youth of Sri Lanka to compete at their best, express themselves, make friends, and build networks that last well beyond the tournament.”

Beyond Esports, Play Expo is a home for art, pop culture, and technology. The Colombo Comic Expo runs alongside the event, with cosplay on the main stage, independent creators in the Artists Alley, local indie game developers showcasing their games, collectibles and merchandise at the Mega Geek Sale, as well as engaging panel discussions and creator meetups. The Game Dev Pavilion spotlights Sri Lanka’s game studios, indie developers, and students, while the Technology Showcase brings the latest gaming hardware and interactive exhibits to the floor.

Maggi Papare Blast joins Play Expo 2026 as the Title Partner, with Milo as the Beverage Partner. Lenovo comes on board as Technology Partner, while Scope Cinemas is the Cinema Partner. Tournament registrations are hosted on InGame Esports (ingame.gg), and tickets are available through PickMe Explore and InGame Esports.

Registrations for Play Expo are free. To register and for more details, visit www.playexpo.lk. For more details about the Colombo Comic Expo, visit www.comicexpo.lk.
